utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if you want to caution the witness, remind the witness of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You wonder if I want?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To remind the witness of the oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Yes. I'm sorry, I'm going to have to call you Mr. Number 3, if you don't mind, simply because of the protective measures. The Chamber reminds you that you took the declaration yesterday in I with you promised to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Are you able to understand me clearly in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You will recall that at the end of the session yesterday we were talking about Kijevo. You told us about something that happened in Kijevo in the spring of 1991. Do you recall something happening in Kijevo in around August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August? Well, that's when Kijevo was practically attacked and when it was cleansed of its Croatian population. Actually, the two territories linked up of the Serb village of Polace and the Serb village of Civljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, when you were in Kijevo after the attack on Kijevo, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When entering Kijevo and further along the road, the houses were still in smoke on the left-hand side, and on the right-hand side we got to the police station in Kijevo. We stopped there briefly, and he talked to Milenko Zelenbada who happened to be there. He asked to have the Croat flag removed, the chequerboard flag. He asked me to do that. Then he went further ahead, well, perhaps a kilometre or so as far as I remember. On the right-hand side there was a house next to which there were a lot of policemen, and there were about ten men there standing by the wall. When we got there we already knew there were some prisoner taken there. We heard that through communications, about ten members of the MUP of Croatia. Soon after that, an APC came there. Ratko Mladic was on the APC. They talked about what they would do with those people. Mladic said that as a sign of his goodwill he would take them then to between the Serb villages of Civljani and Vrlika and he would let them cross over to the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, in your answer you said that in Kijevo you said he asked to have the Croat flag removed. Who were you talking about? Who was it who asked that? Just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic asked to have the Croat flag removed, sort of like a trophy, so that he'd have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On at that day did you hear Milan Martic make any statements about the operation or to the people in -- to the Serb people in Kijevo or around Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I don't remember his exact words. When we were there with those people, he congratulated them on the work they did voluntarily. Already then -- I don't know how to explain this actually. It was sort of a relief for the Serb people on the other side. There was a big advantage that there were no more Croats between two Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic say anything about Vrlika?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when Mladic came and when they were talking among themselves, they mentioned Vrlika because Martic -- or, rather, they were talking and they were saying that Vrlika should be dealt with on that day too. This is a very small town, perhaps a population of 2.000, 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say that they said it should be dealt with, how did you understand that? What did you understand that to mean? What did that mean, "dealt with"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be logical to put a question to the witness along the following lines: What did Martic say after that? What did he mean? Was the conversation between Mladic and Martic clear? Did they mention what it was that they actually wanted? Now, the witness is supposed to tell us what Martic was thinking. On the basis of what can he say that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could Mr. Milovancevic please adjust his microphone. We can barely hear him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard what the interpreter said about your microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I think my question is entirely permissible. If Mr. Milovancevic wants to ask those questions on cross-examination, he's perfectly entitled, but I don't think there's anything improper about what I put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, the objection has been overruled and therefore my question stands, and the question I put to you, just to remind you, is you said that they -- they were talking and they were saying that Vrlika should be dealt with on that day. My question to you was: What did you understand that to mean, "dealt with"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood this word to deal with in terms of having another attack. It was called cleansing at the time, liberating the road between Civljani and Vrlika, and through the Serb village of Otisci. Already then while in this conversation, Mladic said something that as a sign of goodwill he would release these ten prisoners in Vrlika. I think that in that way he wanted to deal with the situation peacefully, that they be disarmed, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the word "cleansing" used at the time? Was that used openly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word cleansing was used at the time, but it was used as a military term, cleansing, a territory that becomes clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've also talked about this term -- you've also talked about this term as meaning getting rid of the Croats, getting the Croat population out of there. What was it used in that way at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That term was used on both sides, cleansing the Croat population or, rather, cleansing the terrain from Croat police, MUP, the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I want to get clear on this. Was the term used -- was the term "cleansing" used to mean cleansing the Croat population and all Croat military forces or just one of them, or how precisely was it used? How did you understand it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of cleansing was that it was 100 per cent territory without people. Directly in that case, completely in that case. In case of a conflict between Serbs and Croats, that would mean cleansing Croat villages, that is to say the population and the military and police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I still don't understand. You said that your understanding of cleansing was that it was 100 per cent territory without people. Does it therefore mean that once the place is cleansed it will be uninhabited? There will be nobody on the land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can say that directly for Kijevo. Hardly anybody stayed behind. Only some very old people who couldn't move, perhaps only about ten of them. It was a very big village before that, 200, 300 people. So there was complete cleansing of the population from the territory that was attacked. I'm sorry. Except for the old and weak who could not move, the entire population had left. That was the objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, yesterday you told us that from what you could observe the police and the JNA during this time was working together in close cooperation. Were you able to observe whether there was any subordination? Was the police subordinated to the JNA? Was the JNA subordinated to the police? Were you able to make any observations about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that in the attack itself against the village of Kijevo there was subordination, because the then Yugoslav air force was bombing the village of Kijevo parallel to the artillery that was guided from the sides. Later on, I heard that this was from the conversation between Colonel Djukic and somebody else that this was 155-millimetre and 130-millimetre artillery from the region of Crna Zemlja. I think that this was a perfect example, ideal, ideal coordination on a joint assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And maybe this was something you were not able to observe, and if so just tell us, but were you able to tell whether military and the police were working in coordination or was there an actual formal subordination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about formal subordination. I just know that Martic ordered the police at the beginning of the operations. He asked the police to join the JNA in certain directions and to help them along. In the army at that time, there were still young conscripts about 20 years old -- 20-year-old, and he ordered the police to join the Yugoslav People's Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you told us that in September of 1991, you learned that Martic had been arrested in Bosnia. Did you learn anything about what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know his exact rank. I'm saying that again. It's the same military man. Now, was he a lieutenant colonel or a colonel, because he was promoted several times over a short span of time. It was Borisav Djukic. They went to a village near Bosanska Krupa where Djukic was from originally. Lieutenant Colonel Djukic, Colonel Djukic, I'm not sure of his rank at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, Witness, did you learn anything about what they were doing there at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through conversations later on, I heard -- or, actually, I was told that they travelled up there because Djukic asked that a certain quantity of weapons be dispatched to his village so that they be armed. As far as I understood, they were threatened from the Muslim village of Otoka. I also know that the Yugoslav People's Army mediated, and they were released from prison due to these mediation efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, in 1992 did you hear of something that was referred to as the corridor operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corridor action was supposed to link up through the republic -- or, rather, the territories of Republika Srpska with the Republic of Serbia proper, and that was supposed to be an open road and territorial link with Serbia, and it was called "the backbone," because without that road, without that territory, you couldn't get supplies in. There would be no supplies, no food, no clothing, footwear, fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Life was under threat in a way without that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, what was Milan Martic's role in the corridor operation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went to the corridor with his elite Krajina unit, the best people he could rally, the strongest Krajina unit of the special police. I think the name was called special unit of the police or part of it was called a special unit. And that was the -- those were the special police units. They were JNA units which had been put into a different uniform, and I think that they were then called special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, during or after the corridor operation, did you observe anything coming from the corridor to the Krajina, to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In at least one case while I was in Golubic, or when I was in Golubic, rather, a helicopter landed, MI8. It was the popular 8 helicopter, as it was called, and out of it stepped Milan Lukic, who was a -- in Martic's security at the time, and Tode Sljivar also got off the helicopter with him. Unusually -- quite unusually the helicopter landed in the middle of the football stadium, and when the helicopter doors opened there was a lot of washing machines inside, televisions, some expensive furniture. There was a small motorcycle of the Tomos make. Lots of different things, technical goods, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn where those goods, those things, came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lukic said that they had loaded up those goods from a village Kotorsko towards Johovac, and that it was actually Croatian territory north -- I think it was north of Doboj. They took the furniture out of the house of a doctor who was very wealthy, and they said that they had found a lot of whisky there and that they had drunk a lot of whisky, and they couldn't believe how rich this man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, yesterday you talked about problems during 1991 when the JNA was complaining that the police were engaging in theft, and you told us that Milan Martic was trying to deal with these complaints, and what wasn't clear to me is was Milan Martic concerned about the thefts occurring, or was he concerned about that there were problems with the JNA, or was he concerned about something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the problems at that time -- well, as he knew the JNA commanders well, I think that the main thing was not to upset those relations, because there was tension between the commanders of the army and the police. Not everything ran smoothly or simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic now and to the election campaign in 1993, 1994, Milan Martic's presidential campaign. Did you know how that campaign was financed? Where did the money come from for that election?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion before the campaign itself, he was, that is to say Martic, was in Bosanski Novi for talks with Borislav Mikelic, and on that day he met with Jovica Stanisic in Belgrade. And when he returned, he said that he had received some money, shillings, actually, as assistance to the action -- not action, I mean the pre-election campaign, because very often people who were around him would ask him something interesting, how things stood financially. You see, the people were at breaking point. No more food, no more anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever hear how much money -- any figures about how much money he received from Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can explain this to you in the following way: After his victory at the elections, that day, roughly, and that night he distributed a lot of money amongst his associates, 1.000 shillings. He received 450.000 marks in Austrian shillings for the elections, as far as I know, and there were 20 or 30 people around him and he would give everyone a bonus of 1.000 shillings. And 1.000 Austrian shillings was 1.400 German marks at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, in 1995, did you hear of something calmed Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've told us that Milan Martic said that he told Celeketic to hit Zagreb, Sisak and that area on the day -- that morning after Operation Flash. Now, could you -- on the following day, do you -- did you hear him say anything about Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, he was very angry, and he asked at that Zagreb be hit, Ilica, Ban. He said Ban and the horse. That's actually the square, Ban Jelacic square in Zagreb. And also, he asked for Sisak and Karlovac. And that's why he asked that they be called and that Orhan [sic] be hit -- used, that is to say that Orkan be used. Because Karlovac could not be hit by regular artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So did you hear him say that Orkan should be used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That what is to be used?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Orkan. It's a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just seeing it on the script here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear him say that Orkans, Orkan rockets, should be used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did mention Orkan because nothing else could be used except for another weapon. I think that it was called the war system Luna. Nothing else could reach that. He didn't hide it. He said it quite openly, publicly, in front of television and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you said that he said Zagreb should be hit, Ilica. What is Ilica a reference to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Ilica is a street in Zagreb where -- it's a shopping area where most of the shops are, and people stroll down it. That's how I understand it. Lots of people anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was he saying that the Ilica and the Ban square should be target?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he was angry. He said they don't mind which targets they hit because there are many people who were killed and wounded, and there was general unrest at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, in August of 1995 did you leave the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was that because of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, I'm sorry, can I ask a question about something that happened a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the horse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counter-intelligence. KOS?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think there's a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He understood you -- it was interpreted as KOS and you were asking about horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's on the transcript is said is, if you look at page 16 line 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. I would just suggest if you repeat the question and maybe it will be interpreted correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me do that. Now, what I have here says that you said the next day he was very angry, and he asked that Zagreb be hit, Ilica, Ban. He said Ban and the horse. That's actually the square, Ban Jelacic square in Zagreb. I want to know what the horse and what Ban is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can explain that. It's a symbol of the Croatian people. Ban was a historical personage in Croatia, and he was on a horse, h-o-r-s-e. He's riding a horse. It's statue, a monument in the middle of the square in Zagreb. So when it's this Croatian army leader on a horse or ruler or whatever he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And his name is Ban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His title, a noble title, is Ban, and it is attached to the name to denote nobility. Ban, as I understand it, is somebody who had great respect, great wealth. He was a military leader. I don't know what he actually was, what kind of Croatian personage, but Ban is a title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I'll remind you we're now in public session. Thank you for answering my questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm Predrag Milovancevic, counsel for Mr. Milovancevic Martic. According to the Rules this is the phase of cross-examination so it is the turn of the defence to put questions to you. Since we understand each other, could you please pause between my question and your answer so the interpreters could do their job properly. Have you understood that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note. Could Mr. Milovancevic please adjust his microphone? We can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- that you were accompanying Mr. Raskovic for the first time in 1989 on a religious holiday. Did you hear my question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was a great honour to accompany Mr. Raskovic. Why was that an honour for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was popular among the Serb population. He was a renowned professor of medicine. Secondly, he was the professor of my relative, Dr. Dusan Opacic, a neurologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said at that he enjoyed a high reputation among the Serb population in Croatia. Did that have anything to do with certain political developments? Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me clarify this straight away. I'm not sure whether it was the case at that moment that the Serb democratic community was being formed right then. This was a Serb political party. He was a very popular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the next time you were with him after 1989 was during the rally in Srb. Do you know what it was that was taking place in Srb? Can you explain what kind of event this was? Can you tell us very briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was called the All Serb Assembly. Already then the Serb Democratic Party had been established. At least that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember these political developments from 1990? You just mentioned the All Serb Assembly in Srb. That was the end of July 1990. Were any elections held in 1990 in Croatia? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no, I do not remember directly, if you mean the elections, but I think there were many problems at the time in the municipality of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, that year, 1990, was it a year in which the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, came to power in Croatia after the multi-party elections were held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty. I think that that was the year of the multi-party system, when it was being introduced. That is to say that in Benkovac approximately at that time Tudjman was there within the campaign of the HDZ. He was president of the HDZ party at that time, but I cannot say for sure whether he was president of Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Tudjman, as president of the party, the president of his party, the HDZ, was in Benkovac, and you spoke about some problem. What was it that happened? What is it that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Financial assistance and other forms of assistance were being gathered. I think the man's name was Zeljko Mlinar. As far as I could hear and in terms of what the newspapers wrote and what was on television, as far as I understood things, he had a scar on the left-hand side, and somebody tried to slit his throat. That's what I understood. That is what people were talking about. That is what was on TV. He had become a victim, big time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you present at the time when the Assembly in Srb was held? That was the 25th of July, 1990. That is the day that is registered as the day of that Assembly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So far, you've been asked several times to bear the protective measures in mind, those that are in place. Please be careful when answering my questions, too, things that have to do with you, personally. I'm just reminding you of that. You said that then in Srb at the Assembly you saw many people who you did not know but who you recognised as well-known public political figures; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you listen to what was being said at this Assembly in Srb? Were any speeches made? And what was the subject of these speeches? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, a lot of us -- a lot of people went to Srb. I don't know how many. Thousands of people were there from all kinds of territories. It's not that I really paid much attention to the context of what was being said. Was I there? Yes, I was. As for the talks that I heard, for the most part these were political speeches. I think that at that time there were a lot of talks about the establishment of Serb municipalities, some kind of election activities. More or less about political activities of the Serbs and different attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That speech about the activities of the Serbs, was that linked to any activities on the part of the Croatian authorities at that time? Was that sort of linked, interconnected in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. In fact, I would say that it was one of the responses to what had previously happened in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw Milan Martic for the first time around the 17th of August, 1990, and you're linking that to the date when the barricades were erected. Is that what you said in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on that day you were returning back from your job, and in your statement given to the Prosecution, did you make that statement, that when you returned home that it had been announced over the radio that there was war and that there was a mobilisation on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, counsel is obviously asking a number of questions based on the witness's statement. Normally when that happens the witness is provided a copy of his statement so that he can refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can provide the witness with a copy of the statement. However, certain things were highlighted which were redacted. So if the Prosecutor has a clear copy without any markings, then perhaps we could use that, because we underlined the points we wish to clarify and highlight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have a clean copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd be much obliged to my learned friend of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You raised another issue, Mr. Milovancevic, that the statement that you are having had some things redacted from it, and what I want to know is, is this one an original version which is not redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's not redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is it anticipated that when Mr. Milovancevic cross-examines on the redacted parts of the statement we will go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think it's -- in the event that he cross-examines on anything that might identify the witness we should go into private session. I guess I put my answer that and that is, yes, parts that were previously redacted in the statement. But anything that might identify the witness we should go into private session, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm at a bit of a loss. I would imagine that a redacted part is redacted because it is not meant for the public whether or not that part identifies the witness. If the witness is going to be cross-examined on that part in open session, I'm not sure what was the point of the redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I wasn't clear. I'm agreeing with Your Honour that if -- on the redacted parts of the statement we should go into private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Not only identifying parts. Okay. Mr. Milovancevic, we -- the Chamber will rely on you because you have the statement and you will know what parts are redacted and what parts identify him. We will rely on you to ask for private session as and when the need arises. Is that okay? Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best to bear in mind not to disclose the identity of the witness through anything I say. I'll do my best so that a problem does not arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we reached the 17th of August, or a date around those days with the event called the log revolution, and it is to be found on page 3 of your statement, paragraph 9. Let me repeat the question. So on that day you received information according to which war had been proclaimed over the radio and that there was a mobilisation under way. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it true then that you set out to report to your wartime base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained to us just like everybody else, all adult males in Yugoslavia at that time, that you had a wartime distribution as a recruit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When there's a war or an emergency situation, when people are called to a mobilisation, is it their duty to go and report to a post set for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you did that just like hundreds of other people that you mention in your statement. You say you saw large numbers of people going to rally at the post determined for reporting to the mobilisation call-up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. When you say "you saw large numbers of people going to a mobilisation post," no. When I said that -- I said that when I arrived at the location, or, rather, near the Golubic primary school where the road forks out and branches out into two parts, Golubic to the left, the primary school on the right, and there's a fork in the road there. I apologise if I've got something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Everything is fine. Everything is in order. We just need to make ourselves understood. In your statement, the written statement you gave to the Prosecution, did you say that when you arrived in Golubic that you saw a makeshift house put up there and that you saw a man whom you later established was Milan Martic handing out weapons with a number of other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. And if I might be allowed to explain. When you enter the settlement, since that was a settlement for a work drive on -- when you come into the right there were these huts on the left-hand side. This hut was called the Staff Command or staff -- or the headquarters, and that time -- that name dated back to the youth work drives that were once held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that it was the place where the command and settlement of the youth work drives existed, was that a separate area? Had it been a separate area for a long time, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been in existence, I think, for the past -- well, when the hydroelectric power plant was being built the settlement was also built. So that was in the 1970s, 1979, perhaps. And once the hydroelectric power plant was completed, it became a youth centre. And there were prefabricated houses, but they weren't set apart with any wire fencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went inside and that you saw a prefabricated three-room house where you saw Martic, and that with him were Milenko Zelenbaba, police inspector from Knin, Jovo Mitrovic, whom you later learnt was the commander of the reserve police force in Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that Mirko Zjenic -- Cenic was also in the house and that he recorded the names of the reserve officers who were issued weapons and to which the location they were sent, the unit they were sent to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand the question, I didn't say that Mirko Cenic was in the house recording this. He came outside later on and helped the lists to be compiled of the people to which Martic had handed out weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 you said that among those who reported to the mobilisation call-up there were JNA reservists and police reservists as well and that those who were on the list received weapons and that once they had received these weapons they would sign for it, sign for the weapons they had been issued. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether weapons were handed out to the reserve policemen, only reserve policemen, or to others as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make this clear. The list that I mentioned was the list of the reserve force that existed. And the second point is that they were issued weapons depending on where they lived, where they had come from. So they would go back to their place of residence, to and from the barracks, and so care was taken that equal weapon distribution existed for each of the locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore state that after the proclamation of a state of war was announced over the radio and mobilisation call-up announced Milan Martic, with his people, distributed weapons to the reserve police force from the list of the reserve policemen, according to the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in that youth centre Milan Babic was there as well as other people whom you didn't know at the time. And you said of them that they were, as you said, tried and trusted members of the SDS who were the leaders in SAO Krajina and so on, and the RSK. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this tried and tested term of the SDS means? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't that they were tried and tested only as far as I was concerned, but what happened on that first day or, rather, that first night, individual SDS members left. They tried to get out of all this, and so quite openly, in front of everyone, they engaged in arguments, decided on certain matters, and that there was a great problem between Opacic, Zelenbaba and the others, because they respected Professor Raskovic, and they didn't want to have done what was being done or what was supposed to be done. So these were discussions they had amongst themselves but they were quite open in discussing these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So does that mean that certain members of the SDS were against this weapons distribution? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the SDS or any other part had anything to do with the weapons of the reserve force of the police, or did that come under the exclusive competence of the police, the SUP of Knin in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that at that point in time it had become clear that everything that was happening had been planned, not only by one man, but that a number of people had to be informed of that and that there had to be a long-term plan for the realisation of things like that. And somewhat later on, these matters were discussed openly, publicly. They discussed how to organise the reserve force, what to call it, how to rally the men, how to meet the needs of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know why that day a state of war was proclaimed in Knin? Was there a siren that went off as a sign of alarm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear an alert siren going off, but judging by what was said at the time, the barricades had been erected to protect the Croatian police forces entering Knin and placing the chequerboard on the Knin police station and the emblem on the caps of the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that from the 19th of August to the 2nd of September, 1990, there was a referendum that was called for in Krajina, a referendum for the Serb people in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a referendum because at a certain point in time I personally went with a man who was a member at the time of the

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) And we took up some passages there with the voting slips, with the ballots, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps line 10 ought to be redacted in view of the guidelines given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. May that line 10 please be redacted, the line starting after "I went with him --" including "I went with him," I think, after Nebojsa Mandinic. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please bear in mind that you ought to take care not to mention exactly what you did. So give us a description of your activity, but take care not to disclose your identity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. It wasn't intentional, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I understand that. Do you know that in connection with that referendum that the referendum was banned by the Croatian government and that that is why the sirens sounded on that day? But you say you didn't hear the sirens go off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that there was a referendum which had been banned judging by the stories going round. It was rumoured that it had been banned, but I don't know exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 of your statement, you said that when all this was happening, around that date, the 17th, it's on page 4 of your statement in the B/C/S version, anyway, paragraph 19, that when they events were happening around the 17th of August that the barricades had been erected, made of logs, and that they were erected on the day when the weapons were distributed in Knin and that they were erected in Civljani, Kosovo, on the Vrbnik-Oklaj road, Zrmanja, Djevrske, and Rudale. Is that right, witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that these reservists who were issued with weapons at the Golubic youth settlement, the police reservists were then sent to these barricades; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that these barricades were used for protection. Who were they protecting people from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood things, these barricades were protection from the Croat MUP, the Croat policemen, and in order to prevent them from placing a chequerboard flag on the fortress of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the 21st of August, about some movements of Croat special forces from Drnis and Sinj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say in that context - I don't want to get anything wrong - already at that time I was at the station quite often, and there were very many people who were on the other side of the barricades, if I can put it that way, who were calling and who were talking about the movements of the police forces that were getting closer to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose police forces these were that were moving in the direction of Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police forces of the MUP of Croatia. They were called "redarstvenici."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. This should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, I proceeded from the fact that this part of the text had not been redacted, but if you wish, we can move into private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suggest we do, Mr. Milovancevic, if you don't mind. May we please -- may the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you described those -- those days, the 17th of August, and duty service, you say that in Golubic there was duty service round the clock and that often the accused Martic was on duty there as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that after spending ten or 15 days in Golubic this staff was moved to Oton and that this happened towards the end of August or beginning the September. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say in your statement that it was being said that the JNA would come to Golubic to arrest all of those who worked at the radio and that that's why you had to move out fast?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that there would be arrests all around. I think Dusan Orlovic came up with that or something like that. At any rate, he was the one who had lots of information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain that you heard that the JNA was negotiating with Tudjman and that one of the subjects of the negotiations was for the Krajina Serbs to get a softer -- to follow a softer line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm very sorry to interrupt counsel. It just would be helpful for us and for the witness if when counsel refers to the statement if he could identify the paragraph number that he's referring to, which he's done in the past but has stopped doing. I think that would be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He's nodding. I assume he understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish to thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I put the text of paragraph 18 to you, that is on page 4 in B/C/S. Do you remember my question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat my question? Did you state that you heard that the JNA was negotiating with Tudjman about softening the line of the Krajina Serbs and their general policy and that they were trying to slow down everything that was going on in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- excuse me. That was what they were talking amongst themselves, the people who were there then, people from the party, when they were talking to Martic, and he was there practically around the clock, for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 of your statement you said, somewhere around the middle: "I do not that I that the JNA was involved in the handing out of weapons." Do you mean then, in Golubic on the 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can explain, because soon after that Tolimir and Pecanac came. They were there on at that day, and there were many things that were not logical, and there was total confusion as to who was doing what or, rather, what was going on. It was all around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that it was illogical for you that intelligence officers. JNA should be checking on what was going on concerning the weapons distribution or was it something else that was illogical to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the policy or the approach of the army, of the JNA, regarding all these problems, on the one hand what they were stating and officers were showing up there, I think this led to confusion. There was no logic, absolutely. What was said later about the arrests and the removal of barricades and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that at that time in Golubic there was the -- there was a retired current, the Bogoljub Popovic and retired Colonel Stojko Bjelanovic. Do you think that retired officers have anything to do with the active military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of our mentality and our friendships and what we know, it's the same. When an officer is retired or anybody, he keeps his friends and relationships with people where he spent his entire life before that, which is not to say that they were representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After the news about this possibility of the JNA arresting all of you in Golubic, did you really move to Otok?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning, around 5.00 in the morning, Martic called me. Everything had been packed, and this had to do with the Territorial Defence. And then we went to the locality of Oton. It's actually Oton Polje, top of the hill of Oton, to the Knezovic house. Ratko was one of the brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 19 of your statement, did you not explain that Serb barricades functioned well, that they were equipped with automatic weapons and radio devices and that presidents of local SDS boards were in command, and that Martic also insisted that there be an active-duty police officer at these barricades at all times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I can explain that, too, if necessary. I can clarify what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll move on with the questions and we'll get to that too. Thank you. In paragraph 20, did you say that Martic was really suspicious of the SDS and he did not believe that they were informing him of everything that was going on and he thought that the SDS would not be able to get him the number of people that they had promised for the barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said that openly. Because already at that time, I can just tell you this. Once I said that precisely then when we moved to Oton that there was this division in the SDS. Jovo Zelenbaba -- or, rather, Jovo Opacic and Zelenbaba asked for all this to be closed down before something even bigger happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that local people were at the barricades. Can you tell us what was the point of Martic's insistence that active-duty policemen also be at the barricades? What did he want to achieve through this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the barricades, irrespective of who was travelling in terms of ethnicity, they had very unpleasant situations at the barricades. There were thefts. Money was taken away, their IDs. Whatever they had in their cars would be searched or seized. It was humiliating, and people were very dissatisfied, especially people who were still working then outside the barricades in Drnis and elsewhere. So what was the point? A professional policeman was supposed to supervise this in a way, whereas other people came from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you've said to us just now does that mean that Mr. Martic wanted to ensure law and order by involving active-duty policemen to prevent this kind of wilful behaviour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he really wanted to prevent thefts. And in the beginning his was to have control and prevent dissatisfaction on the part of Serbs who went that way, who worked elsewhere and would come back home that way. Many people worked beyond the barricades so there were many problems involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to what you've just said, perhaps it would be good if you could explain to us. These barricades were actually roadblocks. Did they physically block the road or did they make it possible for traffic to go on but involving certain control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. I can say that on the first day of the barricades they were 100 per cent obstacles. The next few days people couldn't go to work any more. There was nothing. So then these barricades remained, but they got several barricades. Like the letter Z. You'd have to slow down completely. You'd have to go this way and that way. So there were some kind of barriers there or logs that could be moved so they could be closed and opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So, the people that manned the barricades, in the centre where there was a radio station, did reports come in about possible Croatian troop movements? Is that what the people manning the barricades did? Did they send out these messages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that it was the people manning the barricades because each of the barricades had their headquarters or houses, huts. For example, the Vrbnik direction, Oklaj, Vrbnik-Oklaj. The barricade was at the border somewhere. But what happened in the cultural centre in Vrbnik where they slept and what happened in the other villages, for example, sometimes the barricade would be several hundred metres in front whereas the headquarters were in the rear, if I can put it that way. Behind the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said at one point in respect to a question from the Prosecutor that at that time you were not afraid of the Croatian police and Croatian authorities or that you didn't feel fear. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only me but 80 or 90 per cent of the population didn't give it a second thought. We all had friends and relatives on both sides, and there were a lot of mixed marriages, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is it a fact that those barricades were erected to prevent the Croatian police from entering into Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 of your statement, did you explain in the middle of that paragraph or last part of the paragraph, did you say that when two jeeps arrived they were blue police PUCH vehicles when they arrived in Knin, and while you were on your way to the police station you saw members of the regular police force fleeing, running away down the street from those vehicles because they thought that it was the Croatian police? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, why did armed Serb policemen fear the Croatian police? Why were they running away on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that. I can't speak on anybody's behalf. I can't say why they were running away. Most probably they were afraid. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But you said a moment ago that there was no fear. So how can you say that other people weren't afraid or whether they were afraid or not? You see, armed -- you see, these armed policemen when they saw two vehicles who they believed belonged to special Croatian forces run -- tried to run away, ran down the street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was not afraid of this because I didn't give it much thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That will suffice. Did you explain to us that on one or two occasions in Knin people arrived from the MUP of Serbia in order to check out and see whether the police station of the municipality and other important buildings in Knin had been bugged by the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that, as you put it, certain bugs were found in somebody's offices, on somebody's premises? Whose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were found. Mostly -- what I'm saying now is what the experts from the MUP of Serbia showed us. They were found in most offices, in Babic's office in particular, and they showed us what it looked like, like a pea. And they found one, another bug in a vase of flowers. Now, who placed what where, I don't know, but I was present there, so that's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the SUP in Knin and the such of the SAO Krajina at that time, without technical assistance from Serbia, could it have detected those bugs and done away with them, the interception devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the centre in Golubic? Could it provide the necessary vehicles, technical equipment for training without the assistance of the MUP of Serbia that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the people working in the police force? Could they have had salaries without assistance from Serbia, the kind that you talked to us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They couldn't do without assistance from Serbia later on. At the beginning, as I said, their salaries -- other, rather, it was financial assistance that was given and collected by people collecting up money for food, clothing, footwear, meat, meat processed goods, that was given in lieu of a salary, but my answer to you is no, not without Serbia's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether the Croatian authorities abolished any funds from the budget allocated to the Serb municipalities in Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the fact that these funds were cut off, was that the reason that in Krajina there was no resources? There was no money for salaries or anything else, so they needed assistance from Serbia. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether for the salaries of the policemen in Knin that collection drives were carried out amongst the various factories and enterprises in Knin, Tvik, and some other ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Those contributions, were they sufficient to pay out the workers' salaries in the SUP of Knin, for example, or did they have to ask for assistance, financial assistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was enough, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the flights of Croatian helicopters flying overhead? Did you follow this or anybody else in Knin and their -- and the surrounding parts? Was there the threat of Croatian helicopters flying overhead in 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can tell you is that after August 1990, after the barricades were erected there were rumours about helicopters going around belonging to the MUP of Croatia. However, they were flying rather high, so I can't actually say myself, that I saw a helicopter and identified it as being a Croatian helicopter. But I know that a lot was written about that in the papers, by Ljubisa Cvetkovic, for example. So my answer to at that question is yes, there were helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 of your written statement, did you say the barricades in Krajina were abolished at the end of December 1990 or early January 1991, that they were taken down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, did you explain that at that time negotiations took place between the Serbs of Krajina and the Croatian MUP, and that the negotiations were led by a federal commission comprised of the representatives of the federal SUP, the JNA, and the representatives of the SUPs of each of the republics? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the office personally when they arrived, and I said that the representatives arrived. It was the Federal Secretariat of the Interior at that time, and it was made up the secretaries of the SUPs of the republics. And when I said that all the secretaries, that is to say from each republic there was a secretary, and they came to Knin to Martic's office in the police station, and the representative of the army there was a naval officer. Ljubo Beara was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that delegation, federal delegation, that the delegation was established pursuant to an order from the state Presidency in order to calm the situation down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is that the context that you talk about the fact that the barricades were taken down in late December and early January 1991, in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, late December 1990, early January 1991. Well, once the negotiations had started, I can't say on the basis of what these barricades were moved because physically they weren't abolished altogether. They weren't taken down altogether, but the passage was pass -- you could pass by that way. And let me mention just one more thing. At that time, the situation in the Croatian village of Kijevo, as it's downhill, you go downhill, down the road, and it was the village of Kijevo that had set up a barricade first, and also at the exit from Kijevo as you go to the Serb village of Civljani. So that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to Kijevo a little later. In paragraph 26 of your statement, did you say that in January 1991, throughout Krajina police stations were put up and that Milan Martic wanted there to be more stations and more police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say -- when you say that -- you use the term the whole of Krajina, did it comprise six municipalities, Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac, and Lika, Donji Lapac and Korenica and Lika?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the first part that was called the Serbian Autonomous Province of Krajina, which meant all these municipalities which were linked together territorially. Though made a whole, an entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the government of SAO Krajina, in 1991, on the 4th of January, made a decision to establish the SUP of the SAO Krajina and the appointment of Milan Martic as the secretary of the SUP of SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but at the end of 1990 and 1991 many things like that took place. Many things were happening, and I think that in January he became secretary of the SUP of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew that the government established the SUP of SAO Krajina and appointed Martic. Do you know of that particular fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Previously, on the 21st of December, 1990, was the SAO Krajina established with a Statute of its own in Knin on the 21st of December, 1990? That is to say the end of 1990. I'm not insisting upon the exact day, I'm just interested in the general time period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do think it was established at that time, yes. So my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now can you explain to us if the government of SAO Krajina whose representative was Milan Babic passed an order to establish a SUP and brought in a decision to appoint Martic as the head of that SUP, on the basis -- on what grounds do you state in paragraph 26 that this was ordered by Stanisic in order to ensure that the territory stay in Serb hands? Where do you get that piece of information from with respect to the establishment of the police station in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can explain. When I made the statement, we weren't discussing the federal secretary globally and terminologically speaking. The question of people -- of events that were going on, that was the first contact. It was stage two. So the municipalities that were there were there in SAO Krajina. They were Serb territories that hadn't got any connection with the -- with Serbia. They were supposed to establish police stations and be attached, and they couldn't do that without assistance from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As we're talking about this general topic and general context, do you know that in 1990, for instance, after the arrival of Tudjman's party, the HDZ, to power in Croatia, that there was a change in the Croatian constitution and that the Serbs were thrown out of the constitution of Croatia as a nation and that the Serbian language was abolished in the constitution of Croatia as an official language, it was thrown out, and that a new Croatian emblem was introduced, the chequerboard, and that the term redarstvenik was in use? Do you know all about that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't involved in all these events although I do know the term redarstvenik, but I wasn't kept abreast of political events of that kind, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said on the 9th of that are Belgrade there were large-scale demonstrations going on. Can you tell us what year that was and who demonstrated against whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the well-known 9th of March demonstrations that took place in Belgrade where the opposition let by Vuk Draskovic demonstrated against the then power and authority of Slobodan Milosevic. As I understand it, this is my opinion, precisely because of the things that started to happen at that time. And I think they won in 1991, on the 9th of March. They were held in 1991, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is sufficient, Witness. I wanted to ask you this: In paragraph 27 of your statement it says that the demonstrations in Belgrade were held in 1992, 9th of March. So that means that was a mistake. It was a slip, because they took place in 1991, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we've cleared that up. Now, you said that Stanisic called Martic and asked him to send some policemen to Belgrade. Did you indeed say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that those policemen went to Belgrade in a plane, they flew to Belgrade because the corridor was closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the corridor indeed closed in 1991 or was it closed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that the corridor was closed, it was impossible because there was a lot of things going on in Bosnia. It was impossible to have three buses of armed people and take them through Bosnia without them being noticed. So that's what I meant when I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That explanation of yours is somewhat different to what you said in paragraph 27 of your statement, in the continuation of that paragraph, because you say in the penultimate sentence and the last sentence: "Martic told me at that Stanisic had asked for that because the corridor had been closed in 1991, and Stanisic asked that the Serbs in Bosnia be asked to help open the corridor towards Serbia." So that period of time has nothing to do with the events that we know as the events taking place at the corridor, in the corridor, which is April, May, June, 1991; is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, because there was a mistake that was made here. How the mistake came about, I really don't know, but may I be allowed to explain what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I think you and I have understood each other. It's the date that was wrong. So that's enough. That correction is sufficient. And I'm asking you as Defence counsel, I'm asking you this in conformity with the facts that are general knowledge. All I need for you is to say that you agree with that. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this would be a good time to take the break, unless I'm very much mistaken of the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not mistaken. You're just out by half a minute. If it's convenient, then we will take the break at this time and come back at half past twelve. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, a short while ago we spoke about what happened in Belgrade, the demonstrations of March 1991, and what the occasion was. For a moment, we'll go back to the period of August, September 1990. You talked about barricades in Knin, the distribution of weapons, how all of this functioned. You mentioned some organisation called Serb National Resistance. Can you tell us when this appeared and what it was all about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name was the Serb National Resistance, and it consisted of people who were in decision-making positions. For the most part, they were receiving information from the terrain and from radio stations. They were members of the SDS. Dusan Orlovic was then president of Zora, the Serb cultural society. And then there were these others that I mentioned earlier on. Bogoljub Popovic. Former officers of the JNA, that is. Then Milan Martic. It was a body, actually, which had as its task control over the situation on the ground in terms of the movement of Croat troops primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that the full name of this organisation, of this -- or this body was Serb National Resistance Against the Endangerment of Serbs. Do you remember that name, although the -- SSNO is the abbreviation? If you don't remember, just tell me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to say that Serb National Resistance was for creating an organisation for resisting the endangerment of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at meetings of that body, in addition to the persons you mentioned you saw Mr. Babic as well, that he was present often. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first Babic came to the headquarters. All of these meetings took place in this little house that I mentioned at the youth settlement. That's where it all started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This was a meeting -- or, rather, do you know about a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just out of an abundance of caution, perhaps there should be a redaction of lines -- on my screen lines 11 through 15, that is the question "You also said" to the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the Prosecutor is overabundantly cautious. Of course, if the Trial Chamber believes that a further measure of caution should be taken, I don't mind, but I really don't think that I'm bringing the witness into any kind of danger. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That may be true, Mr. Milovancevic, but you are not being denied the right to ask the question. If it is felt by the Prosecution that that might cause a little bit of a problem, maybe we should redact that and then put the same question in private session. And may --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then may lines 11 through 15 please be redacted, and may we move into private session for Mr. Milovancevic to put those questions in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear here, when it's redacted it's only redacted from the broadcast. It remains on the record. So the question and the answer still stands on the record. So I am not sure it's necessary to repeat it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Thank you so much for that clarification. It will stand, but let it be redacted for purposes of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, did I understand this correctly? Are we now in open session or in private session? We should be in open session now, shouldn't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I deal with something now Mr. Milovancevic. At page 66, line 8, previously, prior to that you had asked the witness about Mr. Babic and whether he had attended meetings of the -- of the Serbian National Resistance for Endangerment of Serbs, whether he had attended often. That issue has not been addressed by the witness. Would you like to pursue it? In his answer he didn't address that part of it effectively, I do not believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand that? You described who was there, and then Mr. Babic was mentioned too. Can you tell us when, where? Bear in mind your own position when you explain all of this. When did you see him, how many times? Let's get that clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
