utterances.text: So did you see Mr. Babic at meetings of this Serb national resistance or not? If so, how many times and in what period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to clear things up immediately. When I say meetings, I'm talking about meetings that were not formal ones in the sense of a -- at a given place at a given time. For the most part, behind my back when meetings were being held, two or three metres behind me there was a long table and chairs, and we can say that there were quite a few people there. So let me get that clear. It was not that these were specific meetings that were intended to be meetings. And Babic did come pretty often to Golubic, yes. I'm sorry, I cannot say that Babic came specifically for a meeting, to attend a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about this? Were these meetings called formally or was this a body that was there in view of the nature of the situation? I don't want to lead you in any way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the nature of the situation, people were always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we mentioned the arrival of a delegation which the federal authorities sense approximately in January 1991 in order to calm the situation in the Krajina down. You gave quite a few details about this in terms of removal of barricades. Do you remember, do you know that in January 1991 the Presidency of Yugoslavia reached a decision to have all the weapons that were in the hands of the reserve police returned to arms depots? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was really confused by the first question you put just before this one, when you asked about Croatian politicians and Dr. Babic. I really have no idea about this. What I had in mind was when you're asking me now, that is to say when the federal secretary and the military personnel came, they tried to work something like that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to make the Trial Chamber understand your words when you said "when the secretaries came," could you tell us which secretaries? Could you tell us precisely the secretaries of what so that it would be clear for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said several times that the federal commission, precisely perhaps in this decision that you referred to of the Presidency of Yugoslavia consisted of these secretaries from all the republics, and they made up this commission along with Ljubo Beara, the then representative of the army. Is that the question that you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put another question to you in order to clear things up. It's going to be a direct question. Are you referring to the secretary of the federal SUP and the secretaries of the Ministries of the Interior and the republics? Are these the people that you're referring to? Is this what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to the secretaries from the federal SUP in charge of their different republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. In your statement when answering the Prosecutor's question and also in your written statement, you talked about the camp of Golubic where police specialists were trained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the attendees of that course were, as a rule, professional policemen from different municipalities who came there for special training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that training which gave them advanced knowledge and training also in terms of sophisticated military training which regular policemen do not get. Do not get?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part this was training of military nature for combat units, for combat action, that is. And can I add something to that? There are quite a few policemen there who had previously been dismissed from the police and I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As for the period we're talking about is it 1991, the beginning of 1991, in relation to this training in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was your answer yes? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the first three months of 1991, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state that a man called Frenki, who had come from Belgrade, that he's the one who provided equipment, money for this training camp in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's exactly what I stated, but I said that he first came to Knin at that time or, rather, that he brought this man called Captain Dragan to Knin for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that the trainees, after completing their training, which lasted for two and a half months roughly, went to their own municipalities to the police stations then, that before they left Golubic they had to pass a test of some kind or, rather, carry out an assignment for them to become these specials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also say that every group that went to Golubic for training numbered about 200 men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking all the people that were in Golubic together, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that a platoon which had been trained in Golubic went on assignment to target the Croatian village of Ljubovo in Lika?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecution, did you say that there was some sort of livestock farm in that same village of Ljubovo in addition to the dwellings there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a cattle farm, but it was some sort of farm, yes. Now, it can be a general farm, it can be a factory farm. Anyway, it was a farm of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise if I wasn't interpreting you precisely, but you were speaking of a farm. Right. I couldn't remember the exact words you used. Now, do you know where the position of that farm was, where the farm was located in relation to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that particular farm was on a hill above Ljubovo at an elevation and that it was about one kilometre away from the nearest houses? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at Ljubovo there was a special unit of the Croatian police force precisely on that farm and that it was that farm manned by the Croatian police that was attacked and not a civilian settlement with Croatian civilians inhabiting it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in that action at Ljubovo, the one you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see what the situation was like in Ljubovo after the action had taken place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How come you can claim, then, that there were mortars targeting the houses with the Croatian -- to force the population to flee and to cleanse the area of Croats? How can you say that rocket launchers were fired for heaven's sake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of these stories told by the commander that went on that assignment, and Calic, and the man who rocketed or launched the rocket launchers. He was -- his name was Pero. He was the man who was dismissed, the policeman who was dismissed before 1990. I can't remember his exact surname now, but I will remember it. I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after this attack the Croatian post from Ljubovo was disbanded? Did you hear about that later on, or did you ever hear that at the top of Ljubovo hill, on the former farm, that the special Croatian police force was located there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody ever talked about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that Frenki, who had brought in the resources for work in Golubic, also brought with him instructors, and he devised some sort of armoured train. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain to us that there were about 30 members of the special police force in paragraph 47 of your statement in that train, in that armoured train, and that for the first time the train was used in the attack at Lovinac which otherwise is a Croatian village near Medak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, whether you bet me just explain. Depending on how many people might have been available. Sometimes there might have been 30; sometimes there might have been 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about that attack on Lovinac, and you said that it was a Croatian village, did you also say that in addition to the train there was a mortar company on the other side, a mortar squad, and that Martic was up at the positions as well, 800 metres above the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that armoured train when it went into action on the one hand and the rocket launchers on the other, was the village taken on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 47, did you say that the attack was not successful? "This attack was unsuccessful," is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in Lovinac there was a crew of Croatian ZNG forces, numerous one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain, then, your statement to the Prosecution that the attack was unsuccessful when you had an armoured train on the one side, rocket launchers on the other attacking an allegedly unmanned, undefended Croatian village? Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can explain, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead, try.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, it was a chance to test of train and see what effect could be gained. However, none of the infantry tried to take the village, enter the village. So when I said that Martic was with -- was at about a distance of 800 metres, let me explain. The railway line or the train would go on one side in the direction of the mortar artillery on the other side and we were at a 90 degree angle on the third side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether near Lovinac there was a large ammunitions depot of any kind or a major JNA facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in Licki Osijek there is a large factory for the production of mortars and mines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croatian forces encircled and attacked JNA units and laid siege to them from the ammunitions depot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the attack on Lovinac was unsuccessful. Now, what would you consider a successful attack on Lovinac to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, the success of an attack on Lovinac would have been entry and taking Lovinac -- that the Serbs should take Lovinac physically. But I don't think that the desired effect was achieved, the effect that was planned. And when I say that, I'm referring to the shelling and the effect the armoured train was supposed to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of an inhabitant of Knin by the name of Dambivozar [phoen] in Knin from 1990 to 1995. He looked after the waterworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether a Croat, whether he -- an inhabitant of Knin during all these events from 1990 to 1995, whether there was somebody who drove food round to the nurseries and kindergartens of Knin, food for the children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but Babic's secretary was married to a Croat, and I think she was half Croat herself. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about Martic? Did he ever express any hatred towards the Croatian population or ordered any evil to be done to anyone in your presence or in the presence of other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never directly ordered anything or expressed anything like that. He hated the chequerboard emblem. He hated Tudjman most of all and would imitate him fairly often, but otherwise, that he expressed hatred towards any civilian, no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Milan Martic help the civilian population? Did he protect the civilian population from any ill-deeds regardless of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he tried, as far as I know. He did try. Now, what was behind all that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that not centre at Golubic Frenki arrived to bring in money, equipment, and resources generally. And in paragraph 49 of your statement, you said Martic, Milan Martic, appointed Dusan Orlovic as head of the state security of SAO Krajina. Is that true? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also say that Martic discovered that that man Orlovic was sending reports directly to the state security service in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in contact with Frenki and Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And was Martic angry because of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was angry and more and more distrustful towards them. And, actually, that's what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 49 did you also say that Martic had asked that Frenki be withdrawn from the camp, to Krajina? And in paragraph 52 that at the beginning of 1992 he ordered that Frenki, Captain Dragan, Zoran Rajic Goran Starcevic, Dusan Orlovic be arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 48 of your statement will you day that already in July 1991 Martic was very angry with Frenki?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Because Frenki was constantly flaunting money around and because he was surrounded by people who drank a lot, because he was involved with the local women and didn't leave a good impression on the local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also say that mortars knew about that and was angry because the local population didn't have enough food or fuel, and he wasn't receiving the financial support promised to him, whereas Frenki, on the other hand, was behaving and acting the way he was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned an action at Plitvice in 1991 when it was Easter. Whose Easter was it? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbian Easter, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So who attacked whom at Plitvice on that 31st of March or 1st of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before, Martic had ordered Djurica Djemauz [phoen] to go to Plitvice and to establish a police station there. That night -- that same night or the next day, we saw on television -- I think it was that same day in the afternoon. On television they showed the Serb flag at Plitvice. The next morning, I think there was a clash between the -- well, the Serbian police was attacked by the Croatian police, technically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the majority population at Plitvice? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically for Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Croatian police technically attacked the Serb police. What do you mean "technically"? Who started shooting at whom, and how did it all end? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb police were there. They had taken up their positions the day before. Now, I don't know who started shooting first, but on the Serb side Rajko Vukadinovic was killed. Two other men were injured, were wounded, and two persons disappeared and were later exchanged in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Presidency of Yugoslavia ordered that the Yugoslav People's Army should intervene and separate the two conflicting parties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that it was the Yugoslav state Presidency that ordered that. I don't know what the order was, but I do know that the army was there and that they managed to repulse the Croatian force because they stayed on there for quite a long time, until the end of 1991, the beginning of the war and the large-scale military activities and the cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back for a moment to that 31st of March, 1st of April, 1991. We mentioned Plitvice. We mentioned the Serb side, the Croatian side, the Yugoslav People's Army. At the time was there a war going on in Yugoslavia, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Yugoslavia a sovereign European country, member of the United Nations at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, at that point in time, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA represent the federal armed force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA intervene pursuant to an order from the Yugoslav state Presidency at a point in time when the Croatian special forces were attacking the Serb police on the territory of the state where there is no armed conflict, a conflict broke out between two police forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state again I cannot know who ordered what. I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All I asked you was whether at that point in time the JNA intervened. Looking at the sequence of events and the time involved, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did intervene. Let me just explain. Now, what shape and form this took and pursuant to whose command it intervened, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will go back to the barricades for a moment. You mentioned the barricades, and then you mentioned the barricades in Kijevo. When were they put up, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly now because several times attempts were made to put up these barricades. In January, they became even more and more difficult to negotiate. I cannot tell you exactly, because they put the barricades up several -- in several stages. They would let people go to work, children to school, and then they would put up a total barrier, and then there were talks to the effect of them being closed down completely and open. So it's hard to set a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there Serb and Croat barricades or, to be more precise, barricades on the Serb side and the barricades on the Croat side? Can it be put that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In February or March 1991, as you said in paragraph 31, at a barricade in Kijevo, was Vaso Pecar not killed, a Serb about 20 years old?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Babic went to the village of Polaca from where this killed young man was in order to calm the population down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Babic went to the Serb population in the village of Polaca, whose inhabitant was killed, in order to calm down the situation. Did we understand each other correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Vaso Pecar was killed and who killed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was killed by the policemen, by the Croat MUP. I actually have to explain this. When I say Bat, Bat is the name of a hill, a hilltop. It was half Serb and half Croat. So he was killed below this hill called Bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where were these policemen from and what was their ethnicity, or rather, these people who killed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they were, if they were members of the ZNG or Croatian MUP. But they were policemen at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain where they were stationed? I mean, at what particular place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were stationed in Kijevo. That's when they had established a type of police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So then in February or March 1991 when Vaso Pecar was killed the Croatian authorities established a police station or a type of police station in Kijevo; that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Babic was advised not to go and get the young man's body because that could have been dangerous for him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that some officer of the JNA advised Babic not to go, and what side was the danger on? What kind of danger was involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The danger of him being killed came from the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the body of the killed young Serb lay on the site where he had been killed for two days and that it was impossible to get to him because of that danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the grandfather of this young man, Vaso Pecar, that his grandfather had been killed in the Second World War together with 62 other Serb inhabitants of Polaca and that he was thrown into a pit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, my understanding of redaction is it's not that the statement gets expunged from the evidence but that it is not published to the public, that's all. So may we redact it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is precisely the way I understood you. Yes, that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we redact it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May that sentence refer -- the question saying -- I'll tell you what it is. Page 83, line 15 through to 17, may that be redacted, please. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the killing of this young man of Serb ethnicity, Vaso Pecar, do you know any details about the funeral? Did many people come, and where did they come from? Did they come from Knin only?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a big funeral, yes. Now, I really don't know where all these people came from exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned an action in Kijevo sometime in August 1991. Do you know that at that time the father-in-law of Mr. Babic was killed, that the house of his parents was set on fire and that the mother and grandmother barely managed to save their lives? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot. I cannot. It's hard for me to answer that question. But I do know about people who were killed on the other side. I don't know about this, but I know, for example, in the village of Dragic that two old people were killed, hanged. As for this particularly, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These people killed in the village of Dragic, who were they and who hanged them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this happened, in what period of time exactly? What do you know, and who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot. Well, really, I cannot say now. I know that there were problems to get there, to get them. It's not that I was directly involved. It's not that I knew anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mention Kijevo, Civljani, Vrlika -- Kijevo and Vrlika are Croat villages. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Between them or behind them when facing Knin or the other way around, are there any Serb villages, and did their position pose a threat to the Serb villages in any way? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of Vrlika, perhaps 20 kilometres or so, is the Serb village of Otisci. They had barricades too. They were under a blockade, because from Sinj and Vrlika, I mean they were under a blockade for a long time. That's the only Serb village I know. That's viewed from the east. But if you look on the left-hand side from the east, there are some villages but I really don't know now. Those that -- I don't know what -- or, rather, what kind of villages they are, because most of these villages actually had their populations moved out when the hydroelectric power plant was being built 20 or 30 years ago. So I really don't know who they belonged to eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the population of the Croat villages had problems because of Serb barricades. What about the inhabitants of Serb villages? Did they have problems due to Croat barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Problems in what sense, mutual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mutual. The problems were the same on both sides. You couldn't pass through. You couldn't go to see a doctor. Children couldn't go to school. You couldn't go shopping. So it was both ways. In a way, everybody was tied down to his own village. So what he had there he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Croatian police in Kijevo in February, March 1991 set up a police station there. Are you aware of the history of Kijevo? Do you know that Kijevo was a well-known Ustasha stronghold in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to explain something. Directly, I and many young people did not really pay any attention to all of this. I can say something. A cousin of mine, there is an enormous age difference between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Bear in mind your identity though. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, he was a Chetnik. So we had problems in our relations. So that's why I really find all of this very foreign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Do you know whether in August 1991, in the Croatian village of Kijevo, there was a military police station were there were specialists of the Croatian MUP and the ZNG there at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict when we came after that there was some type of Croatian military there. Now, was it the Croatian MUP, the ZNG, the police or something else, I really don't know. At any rate, it was Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Croatian troops were in Kijevo and how many were taken prisoner, how many Croatian troops on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion ten were taken prisoner. Judging by the equipment and what was there in the station itself, I think there were over 30 people. I have just given an estimate on the basis of the sleeping bags found and the equipment that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a list made of the people who were taken prisoner and that it was 62 of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I can say once again what we saw the first day when the Serb forces entered. There were ten men. I saw them with my very own eyes, and that was when Ratko Mladic was there. And when we came after the cleansing, there were only ten prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what units took part in that operation against Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery support given by the air force, the artillery of the Yugoslav People's Army, then the infantry was the police from the Knin police station, and mortar fire came from Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How come you know all of that when you arrived in Kijevo after it was all over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know simply because the night before the attack was being prepared, the attack on Kijevo, I went to Nebojsa Mandinic. He is a member of the Executive Board of the SDS. And again on Martic orders, we went to the centre of Knin, and Desic [phoen] is the name of that square. That's where we waited for these men with mortars to come from Srb and Donji Lapac. We waited for them and Mandinic and I took them to a locality there of this Boro Djukic, this commander who I already mentioned. We left them there. I think I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This Boro Djukic, whose commander was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just say this: Boro or Borislav Djukic. It's one and the same person. He's a commander from the Yugoslav People's Army in that area. Specifically he held tank positions above the village of Kijevo, and in Polaca on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that this platoon or this unit with the mortar, that you took this unit to Boro Djukic and placed them under his command. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain this. When we arrived, Nebojsa Mandinic talked to them because he was the representative of the then authorities. He said to Djukic or, rather, he introduced the two. I think that Petkovic was the name of the commander of the mortars. And Djukic told him where to place his mortars facing east on the left-hand side. Can I just continue? Now, what was the problem? The problem was, as they said then, that they had 82-millimetre mortars that had a range of only 3.200 metres. So then they started quarreling why they didn't take 120-millimetre mortars so that they could target the centre of the village, because the mortars could not really reach anything else but the first houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Just if there are going to be further questions about this event, I wonder if we could go into private session. It's just sort of specifics about meetings and people and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, may we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned officer Djukic and Milan Martic in Otoka, did you know that on the day he was arrested Officer Djukic was going to his native village to attend his own father's funeral and that he was abducted, beaten up, and released before Milan Martic and completely independently of him? Do you know of that detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how then do you link Milan Martic and Colonel Djukic on that particular occasion? How do you know about that, or do you know about that only on the basis of hearsay, indirect conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost I know about that from what the driver said, Nebojsa Stupar's driver, because he was there. That's the first point. Secondly, they talked about things like that, and it's very difficult to explain that but they talked about those things quite openly. And the third point is that they were in the same vehicle. And if they were in the same vehicle, then I don't think ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us who was in the same vehicle? Do you mean to say that Mr. Djukic, Officer Djukic, was with Milan Martic in the same car or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood the situation, this is what it was: There was a military vehicle belonging to Djukic and Martic's driver. But I state again I'm just telling you what I know and what I was told. So I can't say, because they would talk about that quite often, and that's what stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the Chamber can understand one little point, you say there was a military vehicle belonging to Djukic and Martic's driver. Was it owned by two people? Actually, three, the military, Djukic, and Martic's driver. What do you mean by that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. When I said that, I meant the driver and Martic's vehicle and Djukic, and the vehicle that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army and his driver. So the vehicle belonging to the Yugoslav people's Army and another vehicle that belonged to the police of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there were two vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as I understand it, two vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, who was in the one vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two of them. Martic and Djukic were in one vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who was in the other vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the other vehicle. So there was one driver driving Djukic and Martic, and the other driver was on his own. I don't know that there was a third person involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least that point is clear for whatever --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection to the event in Otoka, have you ever heard of Lieutenant Colonel Smiljanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, whether you know that the -- that Croatia and Slovenia declared their secession from Yugoslavia on the 25th of June, 1991? Do you know about that detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, we're getting no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: English. Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now I can hear you, but the answer was not translated. I think the witness referred to something on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness -- yes, I apologise?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to interpret what the witness said about television?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you repeat the comment you made a little earlier about television, Mr. Witness? Maybe you can repeat the question, Mr. Milovancevic, if you could remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, there was -- there's -- a problem arose with the transcript, so I have to repeat the question, and I asked you this: I asked you whether you heard about the decision of Slovenia and Croatia to secede, and your answer was what? Would you repeat it for the Trial Chamber? When did you hear about that and how did you come to hear of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I only know about it from television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The news on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this would be an opportune moment to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of March 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
